title: Spread along a direction
summary: Centre five points, then compare how far they spread along a few guessed directions.

blocks.title: Five points, one question
blocks.body:
Five points: $(0, 2)$, $(3, 0)$, $(5, 0)$, $(5, 4)$, $(7, 4)$.

Principal component analysis (PCA) asks: **along which direction do they spread out most?** That direction is the best one-number summary of each point.

You will guess a few directions and score them, as you did with lines. Then the next lessons find the best one, and it turns out to be the SVD you already know. Every number here works out by hand.

widget.name: pca-scatter
widget.caption: Drag a handle to turn the line; the dashes drop each point onto it.

blocks.title: The mean

define.meaning: The average point: the average of the $x$-coordinates and the average of the $y$-coordinates. Write it $\bar x$.

blocks.why: PCA measures spread around the middle of the data, so the middle comes first.
blocks.prompt: What is the mean of the five points $(0, 2)$, $(3, 0)$, $(5, 0)$, $(5, 4)$, $(7, 4)$?

slips.say: Divide by the number of points, 5. The $n - 1$ comes later, for variances.

hints: Add the five $x$-coordinates, then divide by how many points there are. Then the same for $y$.
The $x$'s add to 20 and the $y$'s to 10.

check.say: The mean is the cross in the first picture. It should sit in the middle of the cloud.

blocks.title: Centre the x's

define.meaning: Subtracting the mean from every point. The centred points have mean $(0, 0)$: the cloud is moved so its middle is the origin.

blocks.why: Variance is spread around the mean. Centring puts the mean at the origin, so every direction can start from $(0, 0)$.
blocks.prompt: Subtract the mean $x$ (which is 4) from each $x$-coordinate, in the order the points are listed.
hints: Take 4 from each $x$: point minus mean.

check.say: Centred values always add up to 0. Add yours.

blocks.title: Centre the y's
blocks.why: With both columns centred you have the data matrix every later step uses.
blocks.prompt: Subtract the mean $y$ (which is 2) from each $y$-coordinate, in the same order.
blocks.solution: The centred points, one per row, are the matrix $X = \begin{bmatrix}-4&0\\-1&-2\\1&-2\\1&2\\3&2\end{bmatrix}$. Write its rows $x_1, \ldots, x_5$.
blocks.next: Measure the spread along each axis

blocks.title: Spread along x and along y

define.meaning: For a unit vector $u$, each centred point's coordinate along $u$ is $x_i \cdot u$. The variance along $u$ is $\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (x_i \cdot u)^2$.
This course divides by $n - 1 = 4$, the sample convention (numpy's `np.cov` does the same). Dividing by $n$ would scale every variance by $\frac45$ and pick the same best direction.

blocks.why: The two axes are the first two guesses. Their scores are what the best direction has to beat.
blocks.prompt: For $u = (1, 0)$, $x_i \cdot u$ is just the centred $x$. Find the variance along $(1, 0)$ and along $(0, 1)$.

slips.say: That divides by $n = 5$. This course divides by $n - 1 = 4$.
That uses the raw $x$'s. Square the centred ones: variance is spread around the mean.
That is the sum of squares. Now divide by $n - 1$.

hints: Square each centred $x$, add, and divide by $n - 1$.
The centred $x$'s square to a sum of 28, the centred $y$'s to 16.

check.say: Read "Variance along u" in the picture with the line at 0°, then at 90°.

blocks.solution: The points spread more across ($x$) than up ($y$). But the cloud leans, so a tilted line might do better.

blocks.title: What skipping the centring does
blocks.why: Centring is easy to skip and hard to notice. This is what it costs.
blocks.prompt: You skip the centring and put the raw points $(0, 2)$, $(3, 0)$, $(5, 0)$, $(5, 4)$, $(7, 4)$ into the same formula, $\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (p_i \cdot u)^2$. Which of these change? Tick every one.

options.say: The raw $x$-coordinates are $0, 3, 5, 5, 7$. Their squares add to 108, and $108/4 = 27$, not the 7 you get with centred points. The sum now measures distance from the origin, not from the mean.
The raw $y$-coordinates are $2, 0, 0, 4, 4$. Their squares add to 36, and $36/4 = 9$, not 4.

options.text: The distance between any two of the points
options.say: Centring takes the same mean off every point. That slides the whole cloud without changing any distance inside it: $(3, 0)$ and $(5, 0)$ are 2 apart before and after. Only where the origin sits against the cloud changes.

blocks.hint: Add up the squares of the raw $x$-coordinates and divide by $n - 1 = 4$. Is it still the spread of the cloud?
blocks.solution: Without centring the formula measures spread around the origin, so how far the whole cloud sits from the origin is counted as spread. That is why the mean comes first.

blocks.title: A tilted guess
blocks.why: The cloud leans up to the right. A diagonal line follows the lean; is it better than the $x$-axis?
blocks.prompt: Find the variance along the unit vector $u = (1, 1)/\sqrt2$.

widget.name: pca-scatter
widget.caption: Keep this guess, then turn to 0° and 90° and keep those too, to compare.

slips.say: $u$ must be a unit vector: each $x_i \cdot u$ is $(x + y)/\sqrt2$, so each square is halved.
That is the sum of squares. Now divide by $n - 1$.

hints: For each centred point, $x_i \cdot u = (x + y)/\sqrt2$.
Their squares add to 60. Dividing by $\sqrt2$ before squaring halves that; then divide by $n - 1$.

check.say: Read the variance in the picture at 45°.

blocks.solution: 7.5 beats the $x$-axis's 7, by a little. The lean is real, but $45°$ is steeper than the cloud.

blocks.title: A better guess
blocks.why: Between 0° and 45° there is a direction that does better than both. Score one of them.
blocks.prompt: Find the variance along the unit vector $u = (2, 1)/\sqrt5$, about 27° up.

widget.name: pca-scatter
widget.caption: Keep this guess, then turn the line and look for anything that beats it.

slips.say: $u$ must be a unit vector: divide each $x_i \cdot (2, 1)$ by $\sqrt5$ before squaring, so the sum is divided by 5.
That is the sum of squares. Now divide by $n - 1$.

hints: For each centred point, $x_i \cdot u = (2x + y)/\sqrt5$.
Their squares add to 160. Dividing by $\sqrt5$ before squaring divides that by 5; then divide by $n - 1$.

check.say: The picture should read about 8.00 near 27°.

blocks.solution: 8 beats 7, 4 and 7.5. Turn the line in the picture: nothing gets past 8. The next two lessons show why, and what this direction is.

blocks.title: Why a tilted line wins
blocks.why: You have scored four directions. This asks what the scores say.
blocks.prompt: The variances so far: $x$-axis 7, $y$-axis 4, the diagonal ($45°$) 7.5, and the $27°$ line 8. Why does a tilted line beat the $x$-axis?

widget.name: pca-scatter
widget.caption: Turn the line: the dashes drop each point onto it.

options.text: The cloud leans up to the right, so a line along the lean has more of the spread along it.
options.say: The points sit up-right and down-left of the middle, and a line along that lean catches more of that spread than the $x$-axis does.

options.text: $(1, 1)$ is a longer vector than $(1, 0)$, so its sums come out bigger.
options.say: Only if you forget to make it a unit vector. $(1, 1)$ has length $\sqrt2$, which would double the variance to 15. Dividing by $\sqrt2$ makes the comparison fair, and 7.5 is what is left.

options.text: A line that passes through more of the points has more variance.
options.say: Variance is not about how many points the line passes through. The dashes drop every point onto the line, and what counts is how far apart those feet are along it.

options.text: Any tilt beats the axes, and more tilt is better.
options.say: The scores say otherwise: $45°$ gave 7.5 and $27°$ gave 8, so more tilt was worse. The best tilt lies between.

blocks.hint: Turn the line in the picture. Where are the feet of the dashes most spread out along it?
blocks.solution: A tilt wins when it follows the lean, and a fair comparison needs a unit vector. The next two lessons find the best tilt exactly.

sideQuest.title: Check it in numpy
sideQuest.body:
Only if you want to; nothing in the course needs it.

```
import numpy as np
P = np.array([[0, 2], [3, 0], [5, 0], [5, 4], [7, 4]])
X = P - P.mean(axis=0)
for u in ([1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1], [2, 1]):
    u = np.array(u) / np.linalg.norm(u)
    print(u, (X @ u) @ (X @ u) / (len(X) - 1))  # 7, 4, 7.5, 8
```
